repos.title: ReSMap: Recasting Satellite Priors for Robust and Accurate Online HD Map Construction
repos.paper_summary:
ReSMap is a camera-satellite fusion framework for online HD map construction that uses satellite images as a spatial prior and as a fallback when cameras fail. The Predict-then-Fuse (PTF) module averages camera and satellite BEV features, weighting each pixel by that branch's own segmentation confidence, with no learned weights. The Object-Centric Cooperative Multi-modal Query (OCMQ) decoder keeps one shared query set, but each layer updates it from camera-only, satellite-only, and fused BEV features, merged by a learned per-token gate.

On the nuScenes geographically non-overlapping split, the non-temporal variant reaches 47.3 mAP at 60 m × 30 m, versus 40.3 for MapTracker (camera-only, temporal). At 100 m × 50 m it reaches 49.9 mAP, versus 36.2 for MapTracker. The paper also claims gains under camera failure, but those per-scenario numbers are not in the provided text, so they are not reported here.

Limitations: the method assumes the satellite image is accurately localized to the ego vehicle, and outdated tiles or occlusion from shadows, tunnels, tree canopy, or tall buildings weaken the satellite prior. The authors leave the occlusion case to future work because public datasets lack paired scenes of that kind.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Satellite images are proposed as offline redundancy for camera-based online HD map construction when sensors degrade.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior fusion designs assume all modalities are reliable, so corruption can pass through fusion and the decoder.

digest_headlines.heading: Method
digest_headlines.headline: Two modules fuse camera and satellite BEV features by prediction confidence and keep modality-specific query updates.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: The temporal model scores 54.9 mean average precision clean and 32.9 with all cameras dropped.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Localization error, outdated tiles, and occluded top-down views are the stated limits of the satellite fallback.

digest_headlines.heading: Acknowledgments and Disclosure of Funding
digest_headlines.headline: Two Korean government grants fund the work, and the authors declare no competing interests.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists training details, original-split and Argoverse 2 results, MapBench robustness metrics, and extra qualitative examples.

repos.title: Learning Where to Look: Observation Policy Optimization for Thinking with Images
repos.paper_summary:
Observation Policy Optimization (OPO) is a reinforcement learning method that trains vision-language models to choose better zoom-in crops during tool-augmented reasoning. It adds two modules to GRPO-style training. Uncertainty-Guided Observation Branching (UOB) scores each zoom-in call by the entropy of its bounding-box tokens, normalizes that score against the question's pre-action baseline, and branches new rollouts from high-scoring events while filtering redundant crops by IoU. Evidence-Localized Advantage Attribution (ELAA) has a frozen visual judge label each crop as Insufficient, Partial, or Sufficient, normalizes these rewards within each branch group, and applies the result only to observation-action tokens.

Training uses the DeepEyes data for 200 iterations. Qwen3-VL-2B gains 10.0, 12.4, and 15.8 points on V*, HR-Bench 4K, and HR-Bench 8K, reaching 85.9, 78.4, and 76.4. Qwen3-VL-8B gains 4.7, 4.1, and 4.3 points, reaching 92.7, 85.5, and 80.8. OPO-8B scores below Qwen3-VL-235B with zoom on V* (93.7). The excerpt ends before the ablation results, so the claim that each module contributes is not verified here. Limitations include dependence on a single frozen judge for the evidence reward and smaller gains at the 8B scale.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Zoom-in failures mostly stem from observation actions, and OPO adds up to 15.8 points for Qwen3-VL-2B.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Related methods reward crop quality or whole trajectories, whereas OPO compares sibling crops and assigns local credit to observation tokens.

digest_headlines.heading: Preliminary Analysis
digest_headlines.headline: Observation errors cause about 74% of Qwen3-VL-8B failures on V*, and box tokens show higher entropy.

digest_headlines.heading: Method
digest_headlines.headline: UOB branches at uncertain, non-redundant zoom events, and ELAA gives sibling crops local advantages on observation tokens.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: OPO-8B scores 92.7 on V* and 85.5 on HR-Bench 4K, and every ablated variant trails the full 2B model.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The conclusion argues that optimizing observation actions directly improves Qwen3-VL-2B and 8B on high-resolution benchmarks.

digest_headlines.heading: Acknowledgments and Disclosure of Funding
digest_headlines.headline: The acknowledgments credit government, national, provincial and university funding and a supercomputing centre.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists the algorithm, benchmarks, training data, prompts, judges, qualitative cases, localization failures and limitations.

repos.title: Do Agentic Policies Need to Look at Every Step? Geometric Abstraction for Reasoning and Action
repos.paper_summary: This paper proposes a 3D geometric abstraction that gives a language model typed, evidence-tagged references to object parts and compact textual checkpoints with metric residuals, all grounded locally from calibrated RGB-D. The model reasons over these symbols and text and requests images only when needed. The method is evaluated in simulation with a SO-100 arm against a Pixel Reasoning agent that works from images. In policy synthesis, held-out test success after the first revision rose from 21.2% to 45.2% on Bridge+cylinder and from 17.2% to 57.2% on Three-cube stacking. On Ring-on-peg, success after the third revision was 38.0% versus 0.0%. In online execution over 50 paired layouts per task, completions rose from 12/50 to 28/50 on Bridge-tower and from 15/50 to 42/50 on Tower relocation. On Ring-on-peg, model-request time fell 49.4% and recorded tokens fell 52.8%. Limitations: all experiments are simulated with regular object geometries, real-world performance is untested, and geometry is estimated with lightweight CPU methods rather than learned perception.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Closed-loop manipulation need not reinterpret raw images at every step; the paper proposes a typed 3D geometric abstraction instead.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior keypoint, value-map and code-policy methods focus on synthesis or repair, not on a persistent evidence-aware scene state for each action.

digest_headlines.heading: Geometric Abstraction as a Reasoning-to-Action Interface
digest_headlines.headline: Typed references are grounded from RGB-D at execution time and returned as checkpoints with metric residuals and evidence status.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Geometric abstraction improves policy acquisition and online completion in simulation while reducing images sent to the model.

digest_headlines.heading: Limitations and Discussion
digest_headlines.headline: Results cover simulated tabletop scenes with regular shapes; real-world sensing, occlusion, and new object categories remain untested.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Explicit geometric state is presented as a practical substrate for agentic robot policies, with images used on demand.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists single-policy test tables, online outcome and cost tables, evaluation criteria, and the geometric implementation details.

repos.title: $Φ$asmaNet: A Staged Spectral Token-Refinement Architecture for Fast Gravitational-Wave Signal-to-Noise Ratio Prediction
repos.paper_summary: ΦasmaNet is a compact neural surrogate that maps the 11 input features of a precessing, higher-mode binary black hole signal (IMRPhenomXPHM) to its phase-averaged optimal SNR in one detector (LIGO-Hanford) at a fixed Advanced LIGO design PSD. Learned input tokens pass through an ordered cascade of attention-based Φ-Stages, each with a subspace-mixing Φ-Refractor module, followed by gated top-down Φ-Feedback iterations. Labels come from PyCBC, with training sets from 10^5 to 10^6 samples. At 10^6 samples, the model reaches 100−MAPE = 98.73% on the held-out test set, 99.29% after monotonic PCHIP calibration, and 99.39% with R² = 0.9998 for ρ > 8. Under a matched protocol, it outperforms MLP, 1D-ResNet, and Transformer-encoder baselines at every scale, using about 732k parameters. On one GPU it sustains about 1.2×10^5 SNR evaluations per second, processing 10^6 injections in about 8.3 s, roughly two orders of magnitude faster than waveform-and-inner-product computation on a 16-core CPU. Limitations: one detector, one PSD, and ρ < 200. Predictions do not transfer to other PSDs or detector networks, and the paper does not include full ablations attributing gains to individual components.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Selection-effect studies need SNRs for millions of injections, and a neural surrogate could replace the per-source calculation.

digest_headlines.heading: The Challenge of Signal-to-Noise Ratio Calculation
digest_headlines.headline: Direct SNR evaluation is costly per source, and the cost recurs at every likelihood step of a hierarchical analysis.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior SNR surrogates use plain multilayer perceptrons on low-dimensional inputs, and the closest package reduces spins to one effective spin.

digest_headlines.heading: Methodology
digest_headlines.headline: Labels are phase-averaged single-detector SNRs at 1000 Mpc, with 11 input features and a log10 regression target.

digest_headlines.heading: Classic Deep Learning Architectures
digest_headlines.headline: Three baselines serve for comparison: a four-hidden-layer MLP, a 1D ResNet with 2 blocks per stage, and a Transformer encoder with four layers.

digest_headlines.heading: $\Phi$asmaNet: A Staged Spectral Token-Refinement Network with Recursive Feedback
digest_headlines.headline: ΦasmaNet refines eight learned tokens through three Φ-Stages and two Φ-Feedback passes, each stage adding a subspace-mixing module.

digest_headlines.heading: Architectural Novelty and Design Rationale
digest_headlines.headline: Authors frame the contribution as staged inductive bias composition, with stage ordering treated as motivation rather than a verified property.

digest_headlines.heading: Training Protocol, Hyperparameters, and Evaluation Metrics
digest_headlines.headline: Every model shares one protocol tuned on the MLP baseline, so the ΦasmaNet comparison uses settings not chosen for it.

digest_headlines.heading: Architectures Comparison Across Dataset Sizes
digest_headlines.headline: ΦasmaNet has the highest post-calibration accuracy at every size, reaching 99.29 at 1M samples versus 98.06 for ResNet.

digest_headlines.heading: Best-model Diagnostics
digest_headlines.headline: On the SNR above 8 subset, calibrated accuracy is 99.39, and inference runs at about 1.2×10^5 evaluations per second.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion
digest_headlines.headline: The authors support ΦasmaNet for simulation-driven selection-effect studies and list its single-detector, fixed-PSD limits.

digest_headlines.heading: Code Availability
digest_headlines.headline: Training code for ΦasmaNet and its three baselines is publicly released on GitHub.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: Appendix lists out-of-the-box results on YearPredictionMSD, Covertype and Epsilon, with no dataset-specific tuning.

repos.title: ProcessPrefBench: Evaluating Cross-Task Transfer of Individual Process Preferences from Naturalistic Human-AI Interaction
repos.paper_summary: ProcessPrefBench is a benchmark for testing whether an assistant can carry a user's process preference from one dialogue into a different task that does not restate it. The preferences come from three months of natural dialogues between two knowledge workers and an AI-discussion product, and the benchmark has 66 source–target cases. Each source is preselected, so the test measures application rather than retrieval. Three models (DeepSeek V4 Flash, Qwen-Max, GPT-4o) were run under target-only, full-history, and distilled-preference prompts, with two generations per case. Judging used a Claude Sonnet 4.6 judge scoring preference realization on a 0–2 rubric, plus a separate task gate. Imperative distilled-preference prompting raised preference scores over target-only prompting by 0.244 points (95% CI [0.177, 0.313]); full-history prompting gained 0.204. Distillation showed no reliable advantage over full history (difference +0.026, p=.451). Fabricated-evidence failures rose from 5.8% under target-only prompting to 10.4% under imperative prompting and 10.1% under full history. Limitations: two users, one product, and a human audit of only 30 answers that does not validate the fabrication contrast.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Users reveal process preferences in dialogue, and ProcessPrefBench tests whether an assistant applies one learned in an earlier dialogue to a new task.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Existing benchmarks test either memory of dialogue or stated preferences, not whether a preference induced from dialogue transfers to a new task.

digest_headlines.heading: Benchmark Construction
digest_headlines.headline: Each case pairs a source dialogue supporting a reusable standard with a same-user target that does not restate it.

digest_headlines.heading: Evaluation
digest_headlines.headline: Three models are tested under target-only, full-history, and distilled-preference prompts, with 1980 answers generated in total.

digest_headlines.heading: Results
digest_headlines.headline: Full-history and imperative distilled-preference prompts raise preference scores over target-only prompting, but imperative prompting also raises fabricated-evidence failures.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Relevant history improves preference realization, but preserving the right standard and avoiding imported content remain separate requirements.

digest_headlines.heading: Limitations
digest_headlines.headline: The benchmark rests on two users and 66 cases, and the judge audit is diagnostic, so effects hold under the benchmark judge.

digest_headlines.heading: Ethics and Privacy
digest_headlines.headline: Natural interaction traces are not released until participant consent, privacy, provenance, and redistribution rights are reviewed.

digest_headlines.heading: Data and Code Availability
digest_headlines.headline: A public repository holds the benchmark definition, protocols, and schema now, while prompts, code, and case data await review.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists the scoring protocol, judge calibration, sensitivity analyses, two end-to-end case audits, and fabricated-evidence examples.

repos.title: SysPilot: Cross-Library Performance Autotuning via Library Performance Contracts
repos.paper_summary: SysPilot is a cross-library autotuner built on Library Performance Contracts (LPCs), reusable per-library specifications written in the LPCL language. Each contract declares a library's components, the shared resources they use (such as CPU compute and GPU memory), assumptions, controls, and runtime signals. SysPilot composes an application's library contracts, derives resource-conflict hypotheses, profiles the workload to validate them, and generates candidate configurations only for validated hypotheses. An LLM pipeline drafts contracts from documentation and code, and the output is checked against the LPCL grammar. On LibContentionBench, nine cross-library contention benchmarks, SysPilot reaches an average normalized score of 0.960, versus 0.824 for SMAC3 and 0.729 for OpenTuner, and reaches a 0.8 score in 3× fewer trials. On a LibTorch partitioning example, it finds the best configuration in 7 trials, versus 26 for OpenTuner and 45 for SMAC3. Limitations: contract quality depends on documentation, composition is conservative and can yield false positives and negatives, and version and build differences are not handled.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Library composition causes cross-library resource contention, and SysPilot tunes it using reusable per-library performance contracts.

digest_headlines.heading: Motivation
digest_headlines.headline: A two-task LibTorch example shows generic autotuners need 26 and 45 trials, while library-level information finds the best configuration in 7.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: SysPilot complements existing resource-control mechanisms and differs from black-box autotuners by using a structured representation to narrow the search.

digest_headlines.heading: Design
digest_headlines.headline: Library Performance Contracts describe a library's resource use, controls, and signals, and SysPilot composes them into conflict hypotheses.

digest_headlines.heading: Implementation
digest_headlines.headline: A large language model pipeline generates LPCL contracts from documentation and code, and virtual probes keep contracts platform-independent.

digest_headlines.heading: Evaluation
digest_headlines.headline: Across nine benchmarks, contract-guided tuning reaches an average normalized score of 0.960 at 30 trials, above SMAC3 at 0.824 and OpenTuner at 0.729.

digest_headlines.heading: Limitations
digest_headlines.headline: SysPilot's results depend on contract quality, conservative composition may produce false positives or miss undocumented interference, and version sensitivity is not fully handled.

digest_headlines.heading: Future Work
digest_headlines.headline: Proposed extensions include version-aware contracts and distributed workflow tuning, beyond the current single-node focus.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Library contracts with profiling validation find better configurations in fewer trials than generic autotuners.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists the nine benchmarks' libraries, datasets, shared resources, configuration-space sizes, and best performance gains.

repos.title: Flexible Intensities Matter: A Comprehensive Re-evaluation of Hawkes Processes and Neural Temporal Point Processes
repos.paper_summary:
This paper re-evaluates Hawkes processes against neural temporal point processes (TPPs) under one protocol and releases TorchPP, an open-source PyTorch framework implementing both. Hawkes baselines get spline baselines, spline kernels, and an inhibitive variant. Neural models include THP, SAHP, NHP, IntensityFree, and NeuralSplineTPP, a Transformer with a spline intensity head. Evaluation uses autoregressive next-event prediction on five standard benchmarks, plus a 1,257-type UK Biobank disease-history task and a 117-type MIMIC-IV ICU task. Log-likelihood is split into a time term and a type-conditional term. Each model is run with five seeds, and mean and standard deviation are reported.

On the standard benchmarks, flexible Hawkes processes close most of the gap to neural TPPs. NeuralSplineTPP matches IntensityFree and outperforms the softplus-headed intensity models. Added intensity flexibility mainly improves the time term, not the type term. On MIMIC-IV, the flexible neural TPP keeps an advantage in both terms. On UK Biobank, flexible Hawkes processes nearly match the best neural TPP.

Limitations: only next-event prediction is assessed, conclusions rest on seven datasets, and the UK Biobank data and models are not released.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Prior neural-versus-Hawkes comparisons used rigid Hawkes models and omitted medical data, so this paper re-evaluates them.

digest_headlines.heading: Background and Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Hawkes processes sum a baseline and pairwise kernels, while neural TPPs learn intensities from encoded event history.

digest_headlines.heading: Evaluation Design
digest_headlines.headline: Hawkes models gain spline baselines and kernels, and neural models vary only the output head, all under one likelihood.

digest_headlines.heading: Results
digest_headlines.headline: Flexible Hawkes models narrow most of the gap, and neural gains mainly appear in the time term rather than the type term.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion
digest_headlines.headline: Standard benchmarks look dominated by pairwise structure, so a flexible Hawkes process is a sensible practical starting point.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The reported gap was largely an artifact of under-specified models, and flexible intensities also limit neural TPPs.

digest_headlines.heading: Acknowledgments and Disclosure of Funding
digest_headlines.headline: Funding comes from the European Research Council and Deutsche Krebshilfe, and both UK Biobank and MIMIC-IV access are acknowledged.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix covers implementation, EasyTPP comparison, Hawkes baseline reproduction, extra metrics, knot sweeps, and calibration.

repos.title: Twists and Turns: A Graph-Based Benchmark and Framework for Long-Term Memory in Exploration Tasks
repos.paper_summary: LExMem is a graph-guided benchmark for long-term memory in exploration tasks, where a model must track trial-and-error progress toward a goal, including revisions and revived attempts. The benchmark models exploration as directed graphs, evolves them with mutation rules, and instantiates them as 224 multi-turn dialogues (research and software design domains) with 2,018 QA instances in three types: dense subgraphs, sparse subgraphs, and same-type sets. The paper also proposes LExGraph, which segments dialogue into memory nodes with summary-and-fact keys, links them by hierarchical and cross-branch edges, and retrieves nodes by fusing embedding and BM25 rankings, then expanding to neighbors. On LExMem, LExGraph reaches 0.667 F1 and 63.92 ACC on Same-Type questions with Qwen-3.8 27B, versus 0.624 F1 and 61.67 overall ACC for the strongest baseline, LightRAG; the paper reports p<0.05 with paired bootstrap. Limitations: the dialogues are synthetic, and the benchmark tests memory via QA rather than whether recalled memory improves downstream exploration decisions.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Existing memory benchmarks test recall of facts, so the paper builds LExMem for iterative exploration and LExGraph for memory.

digest_headlines.heading: Benchmark Curation
digest_headlines.headline: Graph-guided synthesis turns evolved graphs into 224 dialogues and 2,018 question-answer instances across three question types.

digest_headlines.heading: Method
digest_headlines.headline: LExGraph links dialogue segments into memory nodes with hierarchical and cross-branch edges, then retrieves by hybrid scoring.

digest_headlines.heading: Experimental Setting
digest_headlines.headline: LExGraph is compared with five retrieval-based and three memory-based baselines using token overlap and a judge-scored accuracy metric.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: LExGraph achieves the highest overall LExMem performance across backbones and keeps an advantage on all question subsets.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior memory benchmarks and frameworks target fact recall or semantic and entity links, not the progression of exploration.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Existing frameworks struggle on LExMem, while LExGraph improves on strong baselines and transfers to an external long-term memory benchmark.

digest_headlines.heading: Limitations
digest_headlines.headline: Stated limits are synthetic dialogues and question answering that does not test whether memory improves downstream exploration decisions.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: Appendix lists mutation rules, seed task details, evidence annotation, human evaluation, baseline settings, evidence retrieval results and capability definitions.

repos.title: Spectral symmetry fingerprints in equivariant representations
repos.paper_summary: This paper introduces spectral symmetry fingerprints (SymFP), built from the singular values of equivariant GNN representations at each degree l. For discrete point-group identification, the method counts singular values above a numerical threshold at each degree and matches the resulting rank sequence to rank templates set by fixed-subspace dimensions. For continuous analysis, a leakage score (LS) gives the fraction of spectral energy beyond the target fixed-subspace dimensions, and pLS is its negative log10. A parameter-free equivariant GNN built from radial bases and spherical harmonics lets SymFP run without training. The paper shows that LS cannot increase when moving to a subgroup. Under regularity conditions, rank equality at one parameter setting holds for almost every parameter choice. On a synthetic set covering all 32 crystallographic point groups, degrees 0 to 9 distinguish every group, with identification accuracy of 99.06–100% across HEGNN, TFN, MACE, Equiformer and the parameter-free model. Limitations: rank counts depend on a numerical tolerance, and template matching assumes the representations span the fixed subspaces, which the paper reports for most but not all tested cases.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: The paper treats structural symmetry as two tasks, point-group identification and continuous analysis, and proposes spectral fingerprints from equivariant representations for both.

digest_headlines.heading: Results
digest_headlines.headline: Singular-value spectra of equivariant representations define a fingerprint that matches point groups through rank templates and scores symmetry leakage.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion
digest_headlines.headline: The constraints come from representation algebra, so the framework may extend beyond point groups to space groups and chirality.

digest_headlines.heading: Methods
digest_headlines.headline: Methods define graph compatibility, stabilizers and O(3) representations, and the datasets used for each analysis.

digest_headlines.heading: Data availability
digest_headlines.headline: Synthetic point clouds, Protein Data Bank entries and OpenFF torsion scans are the data sources behind the reported analyses.

digest_headlines.heading: Code availability
digest_headlines.headline: The SymFP implementation, training code and evaluation scripts are released in a GitHub repository.

digest_headlines.heading: Competing interests
digest_headlines.headline: The authors declare no competing interests.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: Appendix lists Extended Data figures and tables on GNN spectra, p97, haemagglutinin, GluK2 and E18 capsids.

repos.title: AttnSR: Attention Step Reward for Long-Horizon Agentic RL
repos.paper_summary:
AttnSR is a step-level reward augmentation method for PPO in long-horizon LLM agent training. It derives intermediate rewards from the policy model's own attention, extracted during actor replay for old log-probabilities, so it needs no separately trained reward model and no additional rollouts. Attention is traced backward from the terminal step through a step dependency graph, with recency correction, layer fusion, and a confidence gate. The outcome reward, relative to a running baseline, sets the sign and scale of the intermediate rewards.

In a controlled study with Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and LoRA training, ALFWorld success rises from 91.2% to 97.1% against terminal-only PPO on 274 held-out tasks. A positional-shaping ablation reaches 92.3%. On ScienceWorld, the method reports higher official scores at all four checkpoints and 29.9% fewer mean environment steps. WebShop shows no statistically detectable gain. Significance uses an exact McNemar test and a paired bootstrap, with one training run per method.

Limitations: attention is treated as a heuristic relevance signal, not evidence of causal contribution, and the shaped return is not guaranteed to preserve the optimal policy. Wall-clock and memory overheads are unmeasured, and the evaluated trajectories are fairly short.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Outcome-only RL gives little per-step supervision to long-horizon LLM agents, so AttnSR derives step rewards from policy attention.

digest_headlines.heading: Problem Formulation
digest_headlines.headline: Terminal-only PPO puts the outcome at the final step, and AttnSR adds signed intermediate rewards without changing that final reward.

digest_headlines.heading: AttnSR: Actor Attention for Step Credit
digest_headlines.headline: Attention is traced backward from the final step, gated by confidence, and centered on outcome to set signed step rewards.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Paired tests show the ALFWorld gain at p=0.002, while the ScienceWorld gain does not survive multiple-comparison correction.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Other agent credit methods use rollouts, learned evaluators or value estimation changes, whereas AttnSR changes only the reward interface.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: AttnSR raises ALFWorld success from 91.2% to 97.1% under PPO, with no detectable WebShop gain and one run per method.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists checkpoint scores, ALFWorld family results, hyperparameters, paired significance, trajectory diagnostics and notation.
